question: The Animal Health Law (Regulation (EU) 2016/429) came into force five years ago. Article 25 of the regulation requires operators to ensure that establishments receive animal health visits by a veterinarian when appropriate, using a risk-based approach. It also allows for the Commission to adopt implementing acts laying down minimum requirements to ensure a uniform application of this provision.

To date, no such implementing act appears to have been adopted. This situation has left the implementation of animal health visits at the discretion of the Member States and has led to differences in the advancement of such measures. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission monitor and assess the implementation of Article 25 across the Member States, in particular regarding the frequency, scope and practical content of animal health visits?

What implementation support mechanisms (including non-legislative acts, guidance, exchanges of best practice or coordination tools) are available or envisaged at EU level to support a more consistent and proportionate application of this provision across the Member States?

In light of reported veterinary workforce shortages, particularly in rural areas, what measures does the Commission envisage to support Member States in ensuring the effective implementation of Article 25?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) Animal health visits in accordance with Article 25 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 (Animal Health Law)1 represent an intrinsic part of operators’ own surveillance. The purpose of animal health visits is to support early detection of animal diseases and to provide advice to operators on several aspects of animal health.

According to Article 25, these visits can be rationalised and combined with visits for other purposes. They can also be counterbalanced with operators’ own surveillance. Member States have different structures in place to organise animal health visits, including public-private partnerships working with farmers on surveillance.

For that reason, and after discussions with stakeholders and Member States, the Commission has not adopted an implementing act in particular as regards minimum frequencies of those visits also in order not to interfere with Member States organisational flexibility, and to not create unjustified administrative burdens and costs.

The Commission monitors the implementation of EU food and feed safety legislation, including the Animal Health Law, in Member States by means of Commission audits2. In addition, the Commission launched an evaluation of the Animal Health Law, which is close to completion. The evaluation addresses animal health visits.
